Submitting Patches
==================

Read this before you send anything to the list. It is short, it is not negotiable, and
it has not changed much since 2005.

1. Sign your work
-----------------

Every patch must carry a Signed-off-by line, and that line must give your real name
(sorry, no pseudonyms and no anonymous contributions). The sign-off is a statement that
you have the right to submit the patch under the project licence; it is not a copyright
assignment, and it is not a promise that the patch is correct.

Use the same address in the sign-off and in the From: header. If the two differ, add an
explicit From: line as the first line of the message body, because some mailers rewrite
the header and the archive then attributes the patch to the wrong person.

2. Describe the change
----------------------

Write the message as an instruction to the tree, in the imperative: "make the parser
reject an empty key", not "fixed a bug". Describe the defect before the fix. A reader
three years from now has your message and the diff, and nothing else.

Reference an earlier commit by its abbreviated object name and its subject, like
1a2b3c4d5e6f ("make the parser reject an empty key"). Use at least twelve characters.
Seven was enough in 2005; in a tree this size, collisions with shorter IDs are a real
possibility, and an ambiguous reference in a commit message cannot be fixed later.

3. Send it as plain text
------------------------

Send patches inline, one per message, as plain text. Attachments and quoted-printable
encoding both arrive mangled on at least one widely used mail client, and a mangled
patch cannot be applied. If you cannot make your mailer behave, send the patch to
yourself first and apply what arrives before you send it to the list.

Do not reformat code you are not changing. A patch that reindents a file is impossible
to review, and the reviewer is the scarce resource here.
